newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium financing profitability being eroded.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium financing profitability being eroded.

text.p: Financing aluminium inventories, which in previous years has been highly profitable, is much less attractive now and the practice has also evolved, Dr Alan Heap, commodity analyst at County NatWest Securities said.

Since late 1996 improving aluminium demand, higher interest rates and declining contangoes have eroded the profitability of financing deals, Heap said at the Financial Times World Aluminium Conference.
At current rates a cash/threes contango of $33 a tonne is needed to finance inventory profitably, whereas the contango is now around $24, and, further out, there are forward backwardations.
"Therefore, there is no longer a profit in financing inventory," he said in a speech prepared for delivery at the conference.

Inventory financing has also changed in recent years, and much of the metal is held away from the London Metal Exchange (LME). In 1993, when LME aluminium stocks were at record levels as much as 80 percent was financed, he said.
Now metal is held off-LME in producer yards, at consumers, or in paddocks in the U.S. Midwest, and as a consequence much of this metal does not appear in published statistics.
"Estimates of the size of the financed inventory stockpile vary from 500,000 tones to one million tonnes," Heap added.

Consumer stocks are being financed because they are needed for final consumption, while inventory may also be built for "one-off", such as recent imports by Hungary ahead of joining the European Union.
"But it seems unlikely that inventory is being taken off the LME for the purpose of financing at a profit," Heap said.
